passage: The wedding hall was loud with drums when someone's uncle lifted Lakshmi onto a chair. "Dance for us, little one!" Fifty faces turned. Phone cameras rose. Lakshmi, five, had danced all morning with her cousin Pema behind the curtain, but now her hands went to her face. She peeked through her fingers and tucked her chin. The uncle clapped louder. Pema climbed up beside her, took her hand and wiggled her own shoulders. Lakshmi giggled into Pema's sleeve, then slid down and hid behind her mother's sari.

qa.q: Who lifted Lakshmi onto a chair?
qa.a: Someone's uncle lifted her onto a chair.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi cover her face when the faces turned to her?
qa.a: The sudden attention felt like too much, and she became shy and self-conscious even though she had enjoyed dancing in private.

qa.q: How could the adults have handled it better?
qa.a: Ask her first, or let her dance with Pema among other children, instead of putting her alone on a chair in front of cameras.

qa.q: How did Pema see the moment?
qa.a: She seemed to notice Lakshmi's discomfort and joined her so she would not be alone in the spotlight.

grounding: It shows a child's sudden shyness when a crowd's unwanted attention lands on her.

passage: At her sixth birthday in the society clubhouse, the lights went off and everyone started singing. Shalini had been racing around with Binita all evening. Now twenty grown-ups and children stood in a ring around her, every face looking her way. The candles glowed. Shalini's cheeks went hot. She pulled her frock over her knees, ducked her head below the table edge and whispered, "Stop singing." Binita crouched beside her. "Blow fast and it finishes," she whispered back. Shalini blew, then hid her face in Binita's shoulder, grinning.

qa.q: Where was Shalini's sixth birthday party held?
qa.a: In the society clubhouse.

qa.q: What does Shalini ducking and whispering "Stop singing" suggest?
qa.a: She felt suddenly shy and flustered with everyone looking at her, even though she was happy about her party.

qa.q: What could Shalini's family try at the next party?
qa.a: Let her blow the candles with a friend beside her, or keep the circle smaller, so the attention feels lighter.

qa.q: Why might Binita understand what Shalini needed?
qa.a: As another child she may know that feeling, and she offered a simple way to make it end quickly. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child's hot cheeks and hiding when a whole room's attention suddenly turns on her.

passage:
"Hemant, come, say your rhyme for Chachi!" Nani called.
"No."
"Arre, you said it so nicely to me yesterday."
"Not now." Hemant wrapped himself in the curtain.
Chachi laughed. "Look, he's shy! So cute!"
"I'm not cute," came a muffled voice.
His cousin Dilnaz peeked in. "Want to say it just to me, in here?"
A pause. "Twinkle, twinkle..." he whispered.
"Nice," Dilnaz whispered back. "Nobody else heard."
A minute later Hemant came out, cheeks pink, and went straight to the biscuits.

qa.q: Where did Hemant hide?
qa.a: He wrapped himself in the curtain.

qa.q: Why did Hemant say "I'm not cute"?
qa.a: Being laughed at and called cute in front of everyone made him feel more embarrassed, and he wanted the attention to stop.

qa.q: How could Nani ask differently next time?
qa.a: She could ask quietly first, or let him say it to one person, as Dilnaz did, instead of calling him out in front of guests.

qa.q: What would change if Chachi had just smiled and carried on talking?
qa.a: Hemant might have felt less watched and come out sooner, maybe even saying the rhyme.

grounding: It shows a child hiding from overwhelming adult attention and recovering once the audience shrinks.

passage:
Note by Nandini Ma'am, LKG
It was Keerthana's birthday today. When the whole class stood and sang loudly to her, she covered her face with both hands and slid under her desk. Her ears went red. I lowered my voice and asked the class to sing softly. She peeped out at the end. Later, one-on-one, she happily told me about her cake. 🎂

qa.q: Where did Keerthana go when the class sang?
qa.a: She slid under her desk.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana have covered her face?
qa.a: The sudden loud attention from the whole class may have felt too much, making her feel shy and exposed.

qa.q: Which choice by Nandini Ma'am helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking the class to sing softly reduced the attention so Keerthana could feel safe enough to peep out.

qa.q: How might the classmates see Keerthana hiding?
qa.a: Some may be puzzled, since they meant to be kind, and might not know that big attention can feel uncomfortable.

grounding: Illustrates a young child's sudden self-consciousness at overwhelming attention, in a teacher's note.

passage: At her cousin's wedding in the village, the dhol started and Leela, five, danced in her new lehenga. Suddenly all the aunties formed a circle, clapping and calling, 'Look at Leela!' Someone held up a phone. Leela stopped mid-spin. Her face crumpled, and she ran to her aunt Gurleen, burying her face in her saree. 'Too many people,' she mumbled. Gurleen led her to the quiet steps.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen lead Leela?
qa.a: She led her to the quiet steps.

qa.q: What made Leela stop dancing mid-spin, and how did she feel?
qa.a: Everyone suddenly watching and filming her made her feel embarrassed and overwhelmed.

qa.q: How could the adults at the wedding support Leela next time?
qa.a: They could cheer from where they are without crowding her or filming, and let her dance when she is ready.

qa.q: How might the aunties see Leela running away?
qa.a: They may be surprised, since they meant their praise kindly, and not realise it felt like too much.

grounding: Shows a young child's sudden embarrassment at unwanted attention during a village wedding.

passage: It was Priscila's fifth birthday, and her aunt Astrid had taken her to a café in Stockholm. Suddenly the waiter came out with a cake and a sparkler, and the whole café started singing. Everyone turned to look. Priscila slid down in her seat and pulled her hood over her face. When the song ended, people clapped. She peeked out, cheeks hot, and whispered, "Can we go home now?" Astrid squeezed her hand. "We can eat the cake first, quietly."

qa.q: What did the waiter bring out?
qa.a: A cake and a sparkler.

qa.q: Why did Priscila pull her hood over her face?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by everyone suddenly looking at her.

qa.q: What could Astrid do next time to make a celebration easier for Priscila?
qa.a: Ask her beforehand if she wants a song, or keep it just between the two of them.

qa.q: How might Astrid feel when Priscila asks to go home?
qa.a: A little sorry the surprise went wrong, and keen to make the rest of the treat calm for her.

grounding: Shows a young child's sudden self-consciousness when a whole café sings at her.

passage: At the school assembly, the principal called out, "Kiran, from UKG, please come up! He found a lost wallet and gave it to the office." Kiran, five, walked up the steps. Three hundred faces looked at him. The microphone squealed. He stared at his shoes, his ears going red, and he didn't say a word. Sachin, his class teacher, came up and stood beside him until the clapping stopped, then walked him back to his line.

qa.q: What had Kiran found?
qa.a: A lost wallet.

qa.q: What does Kiran staring at his shoes with red ears suggest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by so many people looking at him, even though it was praise.

qa.q: How could Sachin support Kiran after the assembly?
qa.a: Tell Kiran quietly how proud the class is of him, and ask if he'd prefer praise in class next time.

qa.q: How might the principal see Kiran's silence?
qa.a: The principal might read it as shyness and could learn that some children prefer quieter praise.

grounding: Shows a young child's embarrassment at unwanted attention during public praise.

passage: I'm Himani, Ganga's older sister. At our cousin's wedding, Ganga, who is five, danced in the middle of the floor. Then the aunties noticed. "Look at her! So cute!" They pinched her cheeks, took photos, asked her to dance again. Ganga stopped moving, grabbed my kurta and hid behind my legs. One uncle kept saying, "Dance, na!" She shook her head and pressed her face into my back. I don't know exactly what she felt, but she didn't dance again that night.

qa.q: Who pinched Ganga's cheeks at the wedding?
qa.a: The aunties.

qa.q: What might Ganga have felt when everyone started watching her?
qa.a: She likely felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by all the sudden attention.

qa.q: How could Himani help Ganga in that moment?
qa.a: Stay with her, gently tell the relatives she needs a break, and let her choose whether to dance again.

qa.q: How does Himani see Ganga's change on the dance floor?
qa.a: Himani notices she went from dancing freely to hiding, but only guesses at the feeling.

grounding: Shows a young child's self-consciousness when relatives crowd round her, seen by an older sister.

passage:
Parul's fifth birthday. When the whole family sang loudly and everyone looked at her, Parul hid her face in Papa's shirt and wouldn't blow out the candles. Pranav blew them with her, quietly.
A week later, at a cousin's party. Parul watched the birthday girl clap along. "She's not shy," Parul whispered.
A month later, at another cousin's birthday. When they sang, Parul stood at the side, shy but smiling, and sang softly, not looking at anyone.

qa.q: Who blew out the candles with Parul?
qa.a: Papa, Pranav.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when she hid her face in Papa's shirt?
qa.a: Parul felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by everyone singing and looking at her.

qa.q: How did Pranav help Parul through the moment?
qa.a: He didn't force her; he quietly helped blow out the candles, taking the spotlight off her.

qa.q: How might the family feel seeing Parul hide?
qa.a: They might feel surprised and gentle, realising the attention was too much for her.

grounding: Over a month of birthdays, a five-year-old moves from hiding in embarrassment to joining in shyly.

passage: The Christmas concert had already started when Francis, five, discovered his angel wings were tied on backwards, and there was no time to fix them. He walked on stage anyway. The audience laughed kindly at the crooked wings. Francis turned red, stared at the floor, and stopped singing. Manoj Sir, at the piano, caught his eye, pointed at his own wonky tie, and winked. Francis gave a tiny smile. He sang the last verse softly, then ran off to hide behind the curtain.

qa.q: What was wrong with Francis's wings?
qa.a: They were tied on backwards.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he turned red and stared at the floor?
qa.a: Francis felt embarrassed by the unexpected laughter and attention.

qa.q: How did Manoj Sir help Francis without drawing more attention?
qa.a: He caught his eye, pointed at his own wonky tie and winked, showing that mistakes are okay.

qa.q: How might the audience see Francis?
qa.a: The audience probably found him sweet and didn't mean to embarrass him.

grounding: At a rushed Christmas concert, a five-year-old is embarrassed by laughter and his teacher quietly helps.

passage: On Diwali evening, Sahil's Delhi flat filled with relatives. Every aunty pinched his cheeks and said, "So big now! Say a poem!" Sahil, five, felt everyone looking. His ears went hot. He hid behind the curtain and wouldn't come out. His Dadi, Sharmila, came and sat on the floor beside the curtain. "Too many eyes?" He nodded. "Stay with me. You can say the poem to just me, later." Sahil peeked out, then leaned against her shoulder.

qa.q: What did every aunty say?
qa.a: So big now! Say a poem!

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when his ears went hot?
qa.a: Sahil felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by all the attention.

qa.q: How did Dadi help Sahil?
qa.a: She sat with him, named the feeling, and offered a smaller audience later instead of forcing him.

qa.q: How might the aunties feel when Sahil hides?
qa.a: They might be a little disappointed or amused, not realising the attention was too much for him.

grounding: On Diwali evening, a five-year-old is overwhelmed by relatives' attention and his grandmother gives him space.

passage:
"Jomon, come here!" Neelam called. The carol singers had come to their door on Christmas Eve.

"Why?"

"They want to sing for your birthday!"

The whole group turned and sang "Happy Birthday" loudly. Everyone clapped.

Jomon hid behind Neelam, face red, and covered his ears.

"Too much?" Neelam whispered.

He nodded into her back.

qa.q: Who had come to the door on Christmas Eve?
qa.a: The carol singers had come to their door.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel when everyone sang and clapped?
qa.a: Jomon was embarrassed and overwhelmed, hiding and covering his ears.

qa.q: How could Neelam support Jomon in moments like this?
qa.a: She could warn him before a surprise and let him stay close to her until he feels ready.

qa.q: How might the carol singers see Jomon hiding?
qa.a: The carol singers might find it sweet, thinking he was just shy.

grounding: On Christmas Eve, a child feels embarrassed when carol singers sing for his birthday.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Onam week.

Today Sangeeta won the pookalam competition for our class. When I announced it, everyone clapped and cheered her name.

She went very red, put her hands over her face, and slid down in her chair. She didn't want to come forward for the prize.

I took the prize to her seat instead. She peeked at it and smiled. — Swati

qa.q: What did Sangeeta win?
qa.a: Sangeeta won the pookalam competition for the class.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when everyone cheered her name?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt embarrassed and overwhelmed, covering her face and sliding down.

qa.q: How did Swati support Sangeeta?
qa.a: She took the prize to Sangeeta's seat so Sangeeta didn't have to face everyone.

qa.q: How might the other children see Sangeeta's reaction?
qa.a: They might think she was shy or be surprised that she didn't come forward.

grounding: During Onam, a child feels embarrassed by sudden praise, and her teacher adjusts to help.

passage:
At the temple fair in the village near Kollam, Vishal, five, wandered away from his cousin Jomon.

Soon the loudspeaker boomed: "Vishal, son of Raju from Kottarakara, please come to the stage!"

Everyone turned. Vishal went very red. He hid behind a balloon seller.

When Jomon found him, Vishal said, "Everyone heard my name." Jomon laughed and held his hand tight.

qa.q: Where did Vishal hide?
qa.a: He hid behind a balloon seller.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when his name was announced?
qa.a: Vishal felt embarrassed, going red and hiding as everyone turned.

qa.q: How could Jomon help Vishal feel better?
qa.a: He could hold Vishal's hand, reassure him that it's normal, and not tease him.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel when he found Vishal?
qa.a: Jomon was probably relieved to find Vishal and amused by his embarrassment.

grounding: At a temple fair, a child feels embarrassed when his name is announced over the loudspeaker.

passage: At the Lunar New Year dinner in Vancouver, Grandma said, "Bao, say your new year wish for everyone!" Twelve faces turned toward him. Someone lifted a phone to film. Bao's cheeks went pink. He slid off his chair and pressed his face into his cousin Ada's sleeve. "Too many people," he mumbled. Ada leaned down. "Want to whisper it to me, and I'll say it?" He nodded and whispered. Ada announced, "Bao wishes everyone lots of dumplings!" Everyone cheered, and Bao peeked out, smiling.

qa.q: How many faces turned toward Bao?
qa.a: Twelve faces turned toward him.

qa.q: What do Bao's pink cheeks and hidden face suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by everyone watching him at once.

qa.q: How could Grandma ask next time so Bao feels less on the spot?
qa.a: She could ask him quietly first, or let him share his wish with just one person.

qa.q: What is it like for Ada to help Bao?
qa.a: Ada seems protective and kind, finding a way for Bao to join in without facing all the attention.

grounding: Illustrates a young child's sudden self-consciousness when a whole family dinner table turns to watch him.
